_about: For each past question in questions.json (matched by key: year-paper-mode-70|split): plain, the question in normal English (a string, or {a, b} for a 30 + 40 question); theme, the theme to use (Theme or Issue questions); best, the text that fits part (a); note, a tip for the whole question; picks, the key moments to use from each text (m: moment numbers, 1 to 12, as on the text page; why: what they show; skip: leave this text out). build_eng.py merges these into the questions.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the world of the story is run by men, and how it stays that way.
picks.note: In both Sive and Small Things Like These, women enforce men's rules: Mena and the Mother Superior. That's the best comparison you can make here.

sive.why: Men make the deal and men burn the letter. “You will have no name till you take a husband.”

stlt.why: The women carry all the shame, the fathers are “unknown”, and the priest's house is at the top.

shawshank.why: Leave it out: there are no women in it. The question says at least two texts.

plain.a: In one text, how possible is it for someone to move up or down in society, for example from poor to rich?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Bill climbs from “father unknown” to owning the coal yard, but the nuns still speak only to the better-off parents.

sive.why: Mena is mocked for being poor, and marriage (“the grass of twenty cows”) is the only way up.

shawshank.why: Andy rises from prisoner to the warden's banker, then to a free man.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much characters stepping in to change things made the text feel hopeful or bleak to you.

sive.why: Interference causes the tragedy. Bleak.

stlt.why: One act of kindness saves a life. Hopeful.

shawshank.why: Andy changes the prison and brings down the warden. Hopeful.

plain.a: In one text, did you decide whether it's hopeful or bleak mostly from how it made you feel, or mostly from thinking it through?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Feelings: the shock and the grief decide it.

stlt.why: Both: Eileen's point makes sense (your head), the walk home moves you (your feelings).

shawshank.why: Feelings: sadness for Brooks, joy at the end.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare what people letting others in, or shutting them out, teaches you about the theme.

sive.why: Nanna lets the travellers in and Mena turns them away. Sive herself is shut out: “no name till you take a husband”.

stlt.why: Mrs Wilson took Bill's mother in when her own family wouldn't. Now the town shuts Bill out for taking Sarah in.

shawshank.why: The new men are taunted until one breaks. Andy asks for beers for the whole crew and nothing for himself.

plain.a: In one text, explain how the way a main character thinks helped the writer show that the theme isn't simple.
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Andy says hope is inside you and Red says hope is dangerous. Red is finally freed but isn't free inside.

sive.why: Mike knows the match is wrong but can't bring himself to stop it.

stlt.why: Bill's doubting mind: “wherever you want to go”, and then he chooses.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the people in power stay in control by quietly turning people against each other, rather than openly.

sive.why: Mike blames Liam's family, and Mena lies to Sive that Liam came only to wish her joy.

stlt.why: The nuns favour the better-off, and slip in “places are scarce” with a Christmas card.

shawshank.why: Favours for Andy keep him working for Norton, along with the threat of losing them.

plain.a: In one text, how much does a main character's fear of what happens if they break society's rules change how they behave?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Bill means to “keep his head down”, until he doesn't.

sive.why: Sive can't refuse, so she runs.

shawshank.why: Red says what the board wants to hear and is rejected. He stops caring and is freed.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much showing people as full of contradictions made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Mike refuses the match, then gives in.

stlt.why: A decent man does nothing. A nun offers tea while hiding a girl locked in a shed.

shawshank.why: “Discipline and the Bible”, and the Bible hides a gun.

plain.a: In one text, does the climax (the big turning point near the end) count for too much in deciding whether the whole text feels hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: No: the drowning only confirms it. It was bleak from the start.

stlt.why: The open ending matters more than the climax.

shawshank.why: Yes: the escape wipes out the gloom of Brooks's death.

picks.plain: Pick a theme. In at least two texts, compare how a character ends up complicated and layered because the writer goes so deep into that theme.

sive.why: Mena: cruel, but she was trapped into her own marriage by poverty.

stlt.why: Bill: a good man who first holds out empty hands.

shawshank.why: Red: he wants freedom but has been made to need the prison.

plain.a: In one text, show how the writer looks at the theme so closely that you see both its good side and its bad side.
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Brooks has no hope left, Red warns that hope is dangerous, and hope wins in the end.

sive.why: Liam's plan gives hope, and it is burned.

stlt.why: Fear against hope. He is happy, but he knows he'll pay.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much key characters change their world, are changed by it, or both.

sive.why: Poverty made Mena. The world destroys Sive.

stlt.why: Shaped by Mrs Wilson's kindness, Bill shapes the town back.

shawshank.why: The prison shapes Brooks. Andy changes the prison.

plain.a: In one text, explain whether dealing with the world of the story made a character tougher and better able to bounce back, or not.
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Andy grows stronger and Brooks breaks.

sive.why: She has no strength left to fight back.

stlt.why: His shame turns into strength.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how characters taking or missing chances to learn and get better made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Mike never learns.

stlt.why: Bill learns.

shawshank.why: Brooks can't change. Red does.

plain.a: In one text, use a key moment or two to explain whether complicated or simple things (or both) made you decide it's hopeful or bleak.
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Complicated: no simple villains, and an open ending.

sive.why: Simple: greed kills.

shawshank.why: Simple: good against evil.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the theme made you feel that people are unselfish and put others first.

sive.why: Liam offers to give Sive up if they'll spare her, while everyone else is in it for the £200.

stlt.why: Mrs Wilson's kindness is passed on by Bill, at his own risk.

shawshank.why: Andy risks his life, and later solitary, for the others.

plain.a: In one text, take a key moment where characters deal with each other, and say what it shows you about the theme.
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Tea, a card and money keep Bill quiet.

sive.why: Mike can't look his mother in the face.

shawshank.why: “How can you be so obtuse?”

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the world of the story encourages good values and attitudes.

sive.why: Hardly at all. Good values survive only in the outcasts and Nanna.

stlt.why: Kindness comes from the outsider, Mrs Wilson, not from the Church.

shawshank.why: Friendship and beauty grow despite the prison.

plain.a: In one text, how much does a main character's place in society (rich or poor, high or low) decide how free they are?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: She is sold for £200, and Nanna is threatened with the county home.

stlt.why: Bill made it up in the world. Sarah has no freedom at all.

shawshank.why: Red is stuck. Andy's banking skills buy him room.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the way the theme was handled stuck with you after reading.

sive.why: Her only escape is death.

stlt.why: The barefoot girls, and this really happened in Ireland.

shawshank.why: “Brooks was here”, then “So was Red”.

plain.a: Pick a theme in one text. How new or fresh was what it taught you?
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: A prisoner beats the powerful with brains, using their own crimes against them.

sive.why: The outcasts have no power, but their songs tell the truth.

stlt.why: The nuns have only “as much power as people give them”.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the main beliefs the characters hold shaped the world of the story.

sive.why: Money above all: “men of money… the new lords of the land”.

stlt.why: Respectability and silence: “a finger in every pie”.

shawshank.why: Norton's two-faced faith: “His judgment cometh”.

plain.a: In one text, explain how looking at the world of the story taught you something about people and life.
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: “There's things you have to ignore”, against “any point in being alive without helping one another?”

sive.why: Thomasheen says love is something people like them can't afford.

shawshank.why: People can be “institutionalized”, but something inside can't be taken.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how well the same theme raises questions about right and wrong, and whether those questions are alike or different.
picks.theme: Power and doing the right thing

sive.why: Is a girl worth £200? Mike knows it's wrong and does it anyway.

stlt.why: “There's things you have to ignore.” Bill feels he can't take Communion after taking the money.

shawshank.why: The warden kills to keep his money. Is Andy right to take it?

plain.a: In one text, show how the theme reveals that people are full of contradictions, like being kind and cruel at once.
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Mike is horrified by the match, then agrees to it. Mena is cruel, but she was a victim herself.

stlt.why: A decent man does nothing. A nun offers tea and kindness while hiding a girl locked in a shed.

shawshank.why: “Discipline and the Bible”, from a man who has Tommy murdered.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how the way characters handle a crisis, in their own life or in society, makes the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Mike gives in and Sive runs.

stlt.why: Bill freezes at first, then acts.

shawshank.why: Andy's answer to the crisis is to escape.

plain.a: In one text, how much do kindness and compassion, or the lack of them, make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Mrs Wilson's kindness, passed on by Bill.

sive.why: Almost no kindness, so it's bleak.

shawshank.why: Small kindnesses make prison bearable.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much conflict or tension is used to build up the same theme.

sive.why: The travellers clash with Mena and Thomasheen, and taunt Seán that he'll soon be “travelling by hearse”.

stlt.why: A quiet row at home, and a polite battle at the convent.

shawshank.why: Andy against Hadley, then Andy against Norton.

plain.a: Pick a theme. What did studying it in one text teach you about yourself?
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Would I hold out empty hands? Would I risk my family?

sive.why: Would I go along with something wrong for the sake of peace and money?

shawshank.why: Would I risk punishment to do something good?

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much characters believing that things could be better made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Liam's dream is crushed.

stlt.why: Bill believes he can still choose, and he does.

shawshank.why: Andy's dream comes true.

plain.a: In one text, how did the way love is shown (any kind of love) make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Love “can't be afforded”. Nanna's love and Liam's love both lose.

stlt.why: Family love, which also makes Eileen afraid.

shawshank.why: Friendship as love.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much people are allowed to be different or go against what's normal.

sive.why: The travellers are bullied, and Liam's escape plan is crushed.

stlt.why: Bill was jeered at school and is shunned again at the end.

shawshank.why: Crying gets a man beaten to death. Playing music gets Andy solitary.

plain.a: In one text, how do the people in power stay in power?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Fear, the Bible, violence and murder.

sive.why: Money, and controlling who knows what.

stlt.why: Charm, money and everyone's fear.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how your reaction to the way powerless or badly-off characters are treated made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: The travellers and Sive are treated with contempt.

stlt.why: The girls are locked away, until one is saved.

shawshank.why: Brooks is thrown out into the world and Tommy is killed.

plain.a: In one text, how did people or communities bouncing back, or not, make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Music inside, twenty years of digging, and the beach.

sive.why: The travellers keep singing. Sive can't go on.

stlt.why: A town getting by on little, and one man who finds his courage.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how fair the society is, and whether ordinary people get a say.

sive.why: Sive's future is decided without her.

stlt.why: The Church runs the town.

shawshank.why: The warden is judge and executioner.

plain.a: In one text, how much are people's rights respected, and how much are they under threat?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Wrongly convicted, beaten to death, shot.

sive.why: Taken out of school, and her letter is destroyed.

stlt.why: Locked up, with her baby taken.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how well a big conflict gets sorted out, and how that made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Only by death.

stlt.why: Bill's inner battle is settled, but not the town's reaction.

shawshank.why: Fully settled.

plain.a: In one text, how much did your reaction to the main values in that world make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Money first, the Church's rules second.

stlt.why: Keeping quiet and looking after your own.

shawshank.why: Fear and two-faced religion at the top.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, take a main character making a big decision. Compare what their reasons teach you about the same theme.

sive.why: Money, and Mena's wish to be rid of Sive and Nanna. Mike wants peace.

stlt.why: His shame, and the memory of Mrs Wilson's kindness.

shawshank.why: After Tommy is killed, Andy chooses to escape. Red chooses hope.

plain.a: Pick a theme. In one text, why did it move you emotionally, or why didn't it?
plain.b: In your other two texts, did the same theme move you more, less or the same, and why? Compare them.

shawshank.why: Heartbreak, then joy.

sive.why: Frustration, then shock. It moves you more, because it is so brutal.

stlt.why: Quieter, so it moves you less at first, but it stays with you longer.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare why big change in society does or doesn't happen.

sive.why: It doesn't. Even after Sive dies, Mike thinks of the priest, not of what he did.

stlt.why: Silence keeps things as they are. One man starts a change, and the ending is left open.

shawshank.why: The warden falls, but the system goes on.

plain.a: In one text, how much was an important relationship affected by the world of the story?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Sive and Liam.

stlt.why: Bill and Eileen.

shawshank.why: Andy and Red.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much the parts that disturbed or unsettled you made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: An old man grabs at a schoolgirl.

stlt.why: A girl begs to be taken to the river, and a girl is locked in a freezing shed.

shawshank.why: A man beaten to death on his first night, and Brooks hangs himself.

plain.a: In one text, how much did a character who inspired you make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Andy.

sive.why: Nanna: inspiring, but she loses.

stlt.why: Bill.

picks.plain: Pick a main character in each of your three texts. Compare what in their world decides whether society accepts them or rejects them.

sive.why: Sive: resented for going to school, and “no name”.

stlt.why: Bill: jeered at as a boy, avoided as a man.

shawshank.why: Red: rejected by the board, then lost in a world that doesn't want him.

plain.a: In one text, pick two things about the world of the story that split people apart or bring them together, and discuss them.
plain.b: In your other two texts, compare how divided society is.

sive.why: Money, and how outsiders are treated.

stlt.why: The poor against the better-off.

shawshank.why: Guards against prisoners, then the prisoners together for a moment.

picks.plain: In your three texts, take one main character each. Compare how much their honesty and decency, or lack of it, made the text feel hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Mike can't look at his mother, and does nothing.

stlt.why: Bill is ashamed of taking the money, then he puts it right.

shawshank.why: Andy even launders the warden's money, so he's not spotless.

plain.a: In one text, explain how your own beliefs and values affected whether it felt hopeful or bleak to you.
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: You disagree with Eileen. You agree that people should help one another.

sive.why: People matter more than money.

shawshank.why: Justice and hope.

picks.plain: Pick a main character in each of your three texts. Compare the thing about their world that most decides whether they can be happy or successful.

sive.why: Money.

stlt.why: The Church's power: success depends on keeping quiet.

shawshank.why: Corrupt power.

plain.a: In one text, find something people aren't allowed to do. Why isn't it allowed, and how does society react when someone does it?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Having a baby outside marriage.

sive.why: The same “sin”: Sive's mother's pregnancy still shames Sive.

shawshank.why: Showing weakness, or joy, gets punished.

picks.plain: Compare why the same theme was more entertaining in some of your texts than in others.

shawshank.why: A twist, then revenge. The most entertaining.

sive.why: Seán's foolish song and the travellers' mocking songs: dark comedy.

stlt.why: Slow and quiet. The tension is all inside Bill.

plain.a: In one text, what makes the theme feel more or less relevant to life today?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Poverty, emigration and the fear of speaking out are all still here, and this is real Irish history.

sive.why: Arranged marriages are gone, but putting money before people isn't.

shawshank.why: Wrongful convictions and corrupt power still happen.

picks.plain: In your three texts, compare the main things that changed, or backed up, your first impression of whether the text is hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Bleak from the start, and the ending confirms it.

stlt.why: Bleak at first, changed by the ending.

shawshank.why: Bleak at first, flipped completely.

plain.a: In one text, how much do relationships between characters make it feel hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Andy and Red.

sive.why: Bitterness wins over love.

stlt.why: Bill and Mrs Wilson, Bill and Eileen.

picks.plain: In your three texts, compare how seeing who has power and who doesn't shows you what each world is like.

sive.why: Money has the power. The travellers are powerless but tell the truth. Sive has none.

stlt.why: The Mother Superior against the girls.

shawshank.why: Norton and Hadley, until Andy turns it around.

plain.a: In one text, how far does a main character manage to stand up to the rules of their world, or fail to?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

shawshank.why: Andy wins some, loses some, then wins.

sive.why: Nanna and Liam fail.

stlt.why: Bill succeeds, but at a cost.

picks.plain: Some texts show a theme the way things should be (idealistic); others show it the way things really are (realistic). Compare which way the same theme came across in your three texts.

shawshank.why: The most idealistic: hope wins.

sive.why: The most realistic and bleak.

stlt.why: In between: he frees Sarah, but the book stops before we see the cost.

plain.a: In one text, how much did the theme surprise or shock you?
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: The grab, the burned letter, the drowning.

stlt.why: A girl begs to be taken to the river to drown herself.

shawshank.why: A man beaten to death on the first night, and Tommy shot.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how much groups like families, friends or communities show what the world of the story is like.

sive.why: A family at war, and the travellers outside it.

stlt.why: The Furlong family against the convent.

shawshank.why: The guards against Red's crew.

plain.a: In one text, how much does the world of the story cause a main character's problems, and shape how they deal with them?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Her birth, the burned letter, and the bog.

stlt.why: Bill holds out empty hands, then goes back.

shawshank.why: Brooks gives up. Andy digs.

picks.plain: In your three texts, compare how at least one big event, and how it hit you, made it clear whether the text is hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Sive's death.

stlt.why: The girls in the chapel, then Bill going back.

shawshank.why: The empty cell.

plain.a: In one text, how much does being able to relate it to your own life shape whether it feels hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Using the same text as (a) and at least one other, compare two other things (not the one from (a)) that made them feel hopeful or bleak.

picks.note: Part (b) uses the text from (a) again, plus at least one other. Good “two other things”: the ending (Small Things Like These 12, Shawshank 12) and what happens to a victim (Small Things Like These 7, Shawshank 5).

stlt.why: Family, Christmas, keeping your head down.

shawshank.why: For (b): the ending, and Brooks's fate.

sive.why: Or use Sive in (b): a death that decides everything.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare what the same theme made you think about your own life, and about people in general.

sive.why: Standing up for family. Money makes people cruel.

stlt.why: “Was there any point in being alive without helping one another?”

shawshank.why: Small kindnesses inside, and “Hope is a good thing”.

plain.a: In one text, how far does the ending wrap up the theme in a way you found satisfying?
plain.b: Do the same as (a), on the same theme, in your other two texts, and compare them.

stlt.why: Only half sorted out: we never see what happens next.

sive.why: “Sorted out” by death, which isn't satisfying at all.

shawshank.why: Fully sorted out and fully satisfying.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how hard it is to change the beliefs and attitudes that run deep in that world.

sive.why: Old family grudges, and the Church's rules mattering more than grief.

stlt.why: “There's things you have to ignore”, and “a finger in every pie”.

shawshank.why: “Institutionalized”. “Rehabilitated” is a made-up word.

plain.a: In one text, how much does social class (rich and poor, upper and lower) help you understand the world of the story?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Mena's poor background, “the grass of twenty cows”, and “men of money… the new lords of the land”.

stlt.why: Mrs Wilson “was rich enough to do as she pleased”.

shawshank.why: Class matters least here, so keep this text short. Andy's banker's education sets him apart.

picks.plain: In at least two texts, compare how what you thought of a main character shaped whether the text felt hopeful or bleak.

sive.why: Mike: pity turning to disgust.

stlt.why: Bill: frustration turning to admiration.

shawshank.why: Andy: admiration.

plain.a: In one text, which parts made you feel things, and how did those feelings help you decide whether it's hopeful or bleak?
plain.b: Do the same as (a) in your other two texts, and compare them.

sive.why: Disgust, shock, grief.

stlt.why: Pity, then hope.

shawshank.why: Sadness, then joy.
